content.title: Comparing Scientific Models and Viewpoints
content.overview: In the ACT Science section, you will often encounter 'Conflicting Viewpoints' passages where two or more models (or scientists) offer different explanations for the same phenomenon. Success requires identifying the specific variables each model uses to make predictions and determining where their assumptions diverge.
learning_objectives: Identify the explicit predictors and assumptions used by different scientific models.
Construct a model-feature matrix to compare how models link variables to outcomes.
Identify exclusive predictions that distinguish one model from another.
Determine which model accounts for specific observed data based on its unique variables.

sections.title: The Model-Feature Matrix Strategy
sections.content:
When faced with two models, the most effective tool is a Model-Feature Matrix. This involves listing each model's predictors (the independent variables they claim cause change) and their assumptions. By mapping which observed variables each model links to the outcome, you can clearly see where they overlap and where they disagree. A model 'links' a variable if it claims that changing that variable will result in a change in the final outcome.

![A flow chart showing the steps to compare two scientific models: Identify Predictors, Map Links to Outcomes, and Find Exclusive Predictions.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/fa440c76-9ce9-46c6-8b6a-c22e4a40c5e1-1786506720797-752.webp)

sections.title: Identifying Predictors and Links
sections.content: A predictor is any variable a model explicitly uses to explain an outcome. For example, if Model A says 'temperature determines reaction rate,' temperature is the predictor. To compare links, look at the direction of change. If Model A says 'higher temperature increases rate' and Model B says 'temperature has no effect,' they have a fundamental difference in their links. You must identify which variables are present in one model but absent in the other.

sections.title: Finding Exclusive Predictions
sections.content: An exclusive prediction is a result that one model predicts but the other cannot account for. This usually occurs when one model includes a variable that the other ignores. If two scenarios have the same values for all variables in Model X but different values for a variable only found in Model Y, Model Y will predict a difference in outcomes while Model X will predict identical outcomes.

worked_examples.question: Two models explain plant growth (height in cm). Model X: growth depends only on daily sunlight hours. Model Y: growth depends on sunlight hours and soil nitrogen (N). Data: Plant A (8h sunlight, 10mg N, 12cm growth) and Plant B (8h sunlight, 30mg N, 20cm growth). Which statement best describes a difference between the models?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify predictors. Model X uses only sunlight. Model Y uses sunlight and soil nitrogen. Step 2: Compare links. Both plants (A and B) have 8 hours of sunlight. Because sunlight is the only predictor for Model X, it must predict identical growth for A and B. Step 3: Identify the exclusive prediction. Model Y includes nitrogen. Since Plant B has more nitrogen than Plant A, Model Y predicts a difference in growth. Therefore, Model Y accounts for the observed 8cm difference in growth that Model X cannot explain.

common_mistakes: Assuming that because two models share one predictor (e.g., sunlight), they will always make the same prediction.
Misidentifying a variable as a predictor when the model only mentions it as a constant background factor.
Choosing an answer that claims a model predicts a result based on a variable it never mentions.
exam_tips: Look for phrases like 'depends only on' or 'is independent of' to quickly isolate a model's predictors.
If the question asks which model is supported by a specific data point, look for the variable that is changing in that data point and see which model includes it.
Eliminate choices that claim both models make identical predictions if the data shows a difference that only one model's variables can explain.
content.recap: To compare scientific models, identify the unique predictors each model uses. Use a matrix to track which variables link to outcomes. The key to most questions is finding the 'exclusive prediction'—the outcome that only one model can explain because it includes a specific variable the other model ignores.

knowledge_claims.content: A predictor is a specific variable that a scientific model explicitly uses to explain or determine an outcome.
To compare models, first list each model's explicit predictors and assumptions in separate columns of a model-feature matrix.
A model 'links' a variable to an outcome if it claims that a change in that variable will result in a change in the observed outcome.
An exclusive prediction is a predicted outcome that depends on a predictor present in only one of the compared models.
If two models share all predictors but one model includes an additional variable, only the model with the extra variable can predict differences based on that variable.
It is a mistake to assume two models are identical simply because they share one common predictor.
To verify a comparison, confirm that the chosen difference cites a specific predictor present in one model and absent in the other.
When data shows different outcomes for two subjects with identical values for one variable, the model that includes a second, differing variable is the one that explains the data.
If a model states an outcome depends 'only' on Variable A, it assumes that changes in Variable B will have no effect on the outcome.
In a Conflicting Viewpoints passage, the primary goal is to identify the specific point of disagreement in the models' underlying mechanisms or variables.
When determining which model explains an observation, match the observation's varying variables to the predictors listed in each model.
A model-feature matrix should mark whether a model predicts a positive, negative, or null relationship between a predictor and the outcome.

SCIENCE PASSAGE 4: Pollinator Visits Through the Day
Observers counted visits to equal flower patches during four 30-minute periods. They recorded bee and butterfly visits separately. Weather remained clear, and the patches contained the same flower species and similar numbers of open blooms.

Which prediction is most consistent with the pattern and appropriately qualified?

options.A: All future measurements must equal the last measured value exactly.
options.B: If the same daily pattern continued, visits at 7 p.m. would likely be below the 5 p.m. counts.
options.C: Changing the x-variable cannot affect the measured outcome.
options.D: A single plotted point proves a universal scientific law.

items.explanation: The prediction extends the observed pattern cautiously rather than claiming certainty.

items.stem:
SCIENCE MATERIAL SET 2
Students tested how water temperature affected the time required for a tablet to dissolve. They used identical tablets, 101 mL of water in each cup, and stirred each cup at the same rate.

TABLE 1
Temperature (°C) | Dissolving time (s)
10 | 30
20 | 22
30 | 17
40 | 13

Trial 2 repeated the procedure with twice the water volume. Researcher 1 claims that higher temperature increases particle motion and therefore decreases dissolving time. Researcher 2 agrees that temperature matters but claims that stirring rate is the dominant factor whenever stirring is not controlled.

The researchers agree that:

options.B: temperature is the only factor in all situations

items.explanation: The keyed response follows the material and directly targets 比较两个或多个模型的共同点与差异.

videoLesson.description: Compare predictors, assumptions, and observed variables each model links to outcomes. Create a model-feature matrix, mark linked variables, and find one prediction only one model makes.
